lesson.title: Ears Don't Hear Linearly: Decibels in Audio
lesson.summary: Audio engineers describe gains, losses, and signal levels in decibels rather than raw ratios because human hearing responds to sound intensity in a roughly logarithmic way, and decibels compress the huge range of everyday audio signal levels into a small, manageable set of numbers.
lesson.body:
Recall the general decibel definition: for power ratios, dB = 10 times log10(P2/P1); for voltage ratios measured across the same impedance, dB = 20 times log10(V2/V1). The multiplier differs because power in a resistive load is proportional to voltage squared (P = V squared / R), so a given voltage ratio corresponds to the square of that ratio in power. Because log10 of a squared quantity pulls out a factor of 2 (log10(x squared) = 2 times log10(x)), the voltage form's multiplier of 20 and the power form's multiplier of 10 are really the same underlying relationship, not two independent rules to memorize separately.

Human loudness perception is roughly logarithmic: equal dB steps tend to be perceived as roughly equal-sized changes in loudness, whether they occur near the quiet end or the loud end of the range. That is why the entire span from the quietest audible sound to the threshold of physical pain, a pressure ratio of well over a million to one, is comfortably described using a dB range of roughly 0 to about 120, instead of writing out enormous linear ratios every time a level needs to be stated.

Consider two amplifier output readings taken across the same load: V1 = 1V and V2 = 2V. The voltage ratio is 2. In decibels, 20 times log10(2) = 20 times 0.30103 = 6.02dB, rounding to the well-known audio engineering shorthand that doubling a voltage, into the same load, is a +6dB change. That shorthand is derived directly from the math here, not just asserted.

A second, independent shorthand covers power directly: if a power level itself doubles, the change is 10 times log10(2) = 10 times 0.30103 = 3.01dB, rounding to +3dB. These are two separate reference facts, "+6dB for a doubled voltage" and "+3dB for a doubled power," each useful in its own context, and it is worth keeping them straight rather than assuming one implies the other, since they describe different starting quantities.
